text: Since Sellers was still too ill to work, he asked Waythorn to take charge of an important deal in which Varick had a share. <break time="0.8s" /> It was impossible to refuse without explaining why, so Waythorn found himself meeting his wifes second husband regularly across the desk of his own office. <break time="0.8s" /> Varick behaved with easy good manners, and Waythorn was forced to admit that the man was far easier to deal with than he had expected. <break time="0.8s" /> Meanwhile Haskett continued his visits to his recovering daughter, and one afternoon, coming home early, Waythorn found him waiting alone in the library of his own house. <break time="0.8s" /> He was a small, effaced looking man with a thin gray beard, whose shabby respectability made it hard to believe that Alice had once been his wife. <break time="0.8s" /> Waythorns eye was caught by his tie, a made up tie fastened with an elastic, and that small detail seemed to tell the whole story of Hasketts life. <break time="0.8s" /> He suddenly pictured Alice as Missus Haskett, sitting in a plush furnished front parlor in Utica and pushing a baby carriage along the street on Sunday afternoons. <break time="0.8s" /> The picture troubled him deeply, for if she had once fitted so easily into that life, how many other lives might she have fitted into just as easily. <break time="0.8s" /> Had he known how lightly she could put aside her past, he might never have felt so secure in the life they were beginning together.
